example:
record = {"a": True, "b": False, "c": False}
evaluate("a == TRUE OR b == TRUE AND c == TRUE", record)
start: Treat it as three jobs, in order: cut the text into tokens (names, `==`, `!=`, strings, integers, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `AND`, `OR`, brackets), check that the tokens form one complete policy, and only then read the record. Splitting on spaces or on the word `OR` breaks as soon as a quoted string contains either.

Recursive descent, one function per precedence level: an expression is AND-groups joined by `OR`, an AND-group is factors joined by `AND`, and a factor is a bracketed expression or `name ==/!= literal`. That order is what makes AND bind tighter. Parse everything into a tree and require the end of the tokens before evaluating, so a broken right branch raises even when the left side is already true.

Evaluate the finished tree with short circuits: for `OR`, look at the right side only when the left is false; for `AND`, only when it is true. A comparison is true only if the field is in the record and `type(actual) is type(literal)`; otherwise both `==` and `!=` are false, so `True == 1` and missing fields never grant access.

start.text: Tokens as `(kind, value, position)` tuples, ending with an `EOF` token, make every rule a check on `tokens[pos][0]`. The OR level, with the rest left to you:

test_precedence_and_parentheses: With `a` true and `b`, `c` false: `a == TRUE OR b == TRUE AND c == TRUE` must be `True`, because AND binds first; `(a == TRUE OR b == TRUE) AND c == TRUE` must be `False`; and `((a == TRUE))` must be `True`, so brackets nest.
If the first one comes out `False`, you are combining left to right as you read. OR has to wait for the whole AND-group on its right: parse AND-groups first, then join those with OR.
test_missing_types_and_strings: A missing field makes both `==` and `!=` false, and so does a type mismatch: with `active` set to `True`, `active == 1` and `active != 1` are both `False`, although Python says `True == 1`. Check `type(actual) is type(expected)` before comparing values.

`name == "A\"B"` holds an escaped quote: decode string literals with JSON's rules (`json.loads` on the quoted text gives `A"B`). `age == -2` needs negative integers, and `user.role` is one field name containing a dot, looked up as the key `'user.role'`.
test_malformed_input_is_not_hidden_by_sh: Thirteen broken policies, each of which must raise ValueError against `{'a': 1}`: the empty string, `a = 1`, `a ==`, a dangling `OR`, unbalanced brackets both ways, `a == 1 b == 2`, `a == 1 OR ???`, the bad escape `"bad\q"`, `a == 01`, `f(a) == 1`, lowercase `and`, and an unterminated string. The failure names the one that got through.

`a == 1 OR ???` is the trap: the left side is already true, so an evaluator that stops early never reaches `???`. Lex and parse the whole text, and check that parsing ended at the end of the tokens, before evaluating anything. Integers follow JSON too: `01` is not a number.
test_short_circuit_skips_record_access: The record is a custom `Mapping` whose `['danger']` raises. `a == 1 OR danger == 2` must return `True` and `a != 1 AND danger == 2` must return `False` without ever reading `danger`: skip the right side of OR when the left is true, and of AND when it is false.

On this class `'danger' in record` and `record.get('danger')` also read `record['danger']`, as does `dict(record)`, so never look fields up ahead of evaluation. Test the argument with `isinstance(record, collections.abc.Mapping)`: a `dict` check would reject this record.
test_resource_limits_and_long_chain: Four checks: 700 copies of `a == 1` joined by OR must return `True`; 101 nested brackets must raise ValueError, since the limit is 100; `lex` on 1,100 comparisons, 4,399 tokens, must raise ValueError, since the limit is 4,096; and a list as the record must raise ValueError.

`lex` is called directly, so the token limit belongs in `lex`. On the long chain, recursing once per OR means 700 nested calls, and two calls per level pass Python's usual limit of 1,000: fold chains in a `while` loop and evaluate with your own stack.

IndexError: Reading `tokens[pos]` past the end: the empty policy, `a ==` and `a == 1 OR` all run out of tokens partway through a rule. End the token list with an `EOF` token, and have each rule raise ValueError when the next token is the wrong kind.
KeyError: `record[field]` for a field that is not there: `missing != "admin"` is evaluated against `{}`. Check `field in record` first; a missing field makes both `==` and `!=` false.
RecursionError: A rule that calls itself before consuming a token, such as `expression := expression OR conjunction` written literally, recurses forever at the same position. Parse the first operand, then loop while the next token is `OR`.

Otherwise it is the 700-comparison OR chain: one or more nested Python calls per operator adds up past the limit. Fold chains in a loop and evaluate with an explicit stack; keep recursion for brackets, which stop at 100.

stopped: A lexer loop never ends when a character matches none of its branches and nothing moves `pos` on: `a == 1 OR ???` in the malformed test does exactly that without a final branch that raises ValueError. A regex token that can match the empty string, such as `\s*`, stalls the same way.

A `while` loop that joins operands with `OR` or `AND` repeats forever if an iteration consumes no tokens: step past the operator before parsing the next operand, and have the operand parser either consume a token or raise ValueError.
passing: All passing. Time a policy near the token limit as your own input: `evaluate(' OR '.join(['a == 2'] * 1024), {'a': 1})` is 4,095 tokens with no true comparison, so every one is checked. Then the README's follow-up on NOT: why would negating today's rule that missing fields are false grant access to records without the field?
